issues.legal_issue: A later validating enactment can cure a defect in an earlier purported vesting of an evacuee’s property, allowing the property to qualify as composite property.
material_facts: A co-owner who held an undivided share in property with non-evacuee co-owners was treated as an evacuee, and her interest purportedly vested in the Custodian under earlier enactments.
The earlier enactments were challenged as beyond the legislative authority of their makers, and the resulting vesting was held invalid by the High Court.

A later amendment provided that property which purportedly vested as evacuee property would be treated as validly vested despite a defect or invalidity in the earlier law, and it validated related Custodian orders.
The later amendment applied to the co-owner’s interest, which was an undivided share in property held with non-evacuees.
issues.conclusion: The co-owner’s interest was validly vested in the Custodian, so the property was composite property within the meaning of the Separation Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(2-A), inserted into the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 by the Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1960, retrospectively validates property that purportedly vested as evacuee property despite defects or invalidity in the earlier law and validates related orders. The Court found it unnecessary to decide whether the deeming provisions in section 8(2) of the 1950 Act or the corresponding provision of the Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, were independently sufficient. Because the interest was an evacuee’s undivided share held with non-evacuees, it met the definition of composite property in section 2(d) of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951. Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P. did not prevent validation because the later enactment operated retrospectively to cure the defect.

rule.if: challenge_to_evacuee_property_vesting and owner_was_treated_as_an_evacuee and interest_purportedly_vested_under_prior_law and later_law_validates_defective_purported_vestings and evacuee_held_undivided_share_with_non_evacuees

predicates.challenge_to_evacuee_property_vesting: A proceeding challenged whether an interest had validly vested as evacuee property.
predicates.owner_was_treated_as_an_evacuee: The owner of the interest was treated as an evacuee under the applicable framework.
predicates.interest_purportedly_vested_under_prior_: The interest appeared to vest in the Custodian under an earlier enactment, although that enactment was alleged to have a legal defect.
predicates.later_law_validates_defective_purported_: A later enactment provides that property which purportedly vested under an earlier law is validly vested despite defects or invalidity in that law.
predicates.evacuee_held_undivided_share_with_non_ev: The evacuee held an undivided share in property together with persons who were not evacuees.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a purported vesting, the owner was treated as an evacuee, a later law validates defective purported vestings, and the evacuee held an undivided share with non-evacuees, the vesting is treated as valid and the property is composite.

issues.legal_issue: Selling an entire composite property and distributing the proceeds proportionately does not violate fundamental property rights when the non-evacuee co-owners will not purchase the evacuee interest and the property cannot be partitioned.
material_facts: The proceeding challenged the constitutionality of selling a composite property under the separation process.
The non-evacuee co-owners were not prepared to pay the value of the evacuees’ shares.
The property included a sugar mill and could not practicably be partitioned.
The other statutory methods of separation were unavailable in the circumstances, and the property was sold by public auction with the proceeds allocated according to the parties’ shares.
issues.conclusion: The sale of the property and distribution of the proceeds did not violate the constitutional protections against deprivation of property or restrictions on the right to property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(a) of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, authorizes the Competent Officer to separate evacuee and claimant interests through the alternatives specified there, including sale of the property and distribution of proceeds. Where the co-owners will not purchase the evacuee interest and the property cannot be partitioned, sale and proportional distribution are not unreasonable and do not amount to deprivation without authority of law or violate Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this ruling.

rule.if: fundamental_rights_challenge_to_sale_of_composite_property and non_evacuee_coowners_declined_to_buy_evacuee_interest and property_cannot_be_partitioned and other_separation_methods_are_unavailable and sale_proceeds_are_distributed_proportionately

predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge_to_sale_of_: A proceeding challenged the sale of an entire composite property as a violation of fundamental property rights.
predicates.non_evacuee_coowners_declined_to_buy_eva: The non-evacuee co-owners declined to pay for the evacuees’ interest in the property.
predicates.property_cannot_be_partitioned: The nature of the property made physical partition impracticable.
predicates.other_separation_methods_are_unavailable: The other available methods for separating the interests could not be used in the circumstances.
predicates.sale_proceeds_are_distributed_proportion: The property is sold and the proceeds are divided in proportion to the evacuee and non-evacuee interests.

issues.definition: When a fundamental-rights challenge concerns a sale of composite property, the non-evacuee co-owners declined to buy the evacuee interest, the property cannot be partitioned, other separation methods are unavailable, and the proceeds are distributed proportionately, the sale and distribution are not unconstitutional.
